task: I'm the best man at my brother Dan's wedding Saturday and need a 2-minute toast. We met in college, he's always been the one who fixes things for everyone, and he proposed on a frozen lake in Minnesota. Keep it warm, a little funny, and not too long.
rewrite:
ambition:     Build the toast around one specific story that shows Dan as the fixer, then turn it so the fixer meets the one thing he can't fix and doesn't want to: falling for someone. The frozen lake proposal is the payoff. End on a short, sincere line and a raised glass.
agency:       Your own memory of a real time Dan fixed something for you or someone else, told in your words. I can't see that from here, so the toast uses the details you gave (college, fixer, frozen Minnesota lake) and leaves one clearly marked spot for the story.
acceleration: Standard best-man structure: a quick opener, one story, a turn to the partner, a toast line. Two minutes read aloud is about 260-290 words. Use a rule-of-three joke, tease Dan lightly, then go sincere.
accuracy:     Read it aloud with a timer and aim for 2 minutes or less. Nothing outside you can confirm the facts, so have someone who knows Dan hear it once, and check that every detail is something you know to be true.

answers.plain:
Here's a toast of about 2 minutes (roughly 280 words). Swap in the bracketed names and details.

---

**Toast**

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm [Your Name], Dan's [brother/best man]. Tonight I get to say nice things about him, which he knows is rare, so he should enjoy it.

Dan has always been the guy who fixes things. Broken bike? Call Dan. Wi-Fi down? Dan. Car making a weird noise, résumé needs a look, someone's heart just got broken at 2 a.m.? Dan shows up, usually with a toolbox and always with a plan. In college, half our friends had his number saved as "Dan (Fixes Stuff)." I'm only slightly exaggerating.

But the thing about people who fix everything for everyone else is that they rarely let anyone fix things for them. Then [Partner's Name] came along. [She/He/They] didn't try to fix Dan. [She/He/They] just made him happier, and that did more than any toolbox could.

Then there's the proposal. Dan decided the best place to propose was in the middle of a frozen lake in Minnesota. Let's be honest: the man who fixes everything chose a setting where one wrong step meant he'd need fixing himself. But he'd checked the ice thickness, of course. Twice. He probably had a backup plan for the backup plan. And [Partner's Name] said yes, which proves [she/he/they] loves him, because that's a lot of cold for one question.

Dan, you've spent your whole life taking care of the people around you. Tonight, we're all here to say we're so happy you found someone who takes care of you, too.

Please raise your glasses. To Dan and [Partner's Name]: may your life together be warm, even when the weather isn't, and may nothing ever break that you can't fix together.

Cheers!

---

**Notes**
- You said you and Dan are brothers but also that you met in college. If you meant that Dan and [Partner] met there, I can move that detail into the toast. Or tell me if Dan is a friend you call a brother.
- If you have a short, real story about Dan fixing something, like a particular car or a particular night, add it after the "Dan (Fixes Stuff)" line. A specific story will land better than my generic jokes.
- Pause after the ice line and the "backup plan" line for laughs. Read it aloud once or twice to check the timing.
answers.nudge:
Here's a toast of about 290 words, which runs close to two minutes at a relaxed pace. I used [PARTNER] as a placeholder for their name. I assumed Dan and [PARTNER] met in college, since you and Dan are brothers. If that's wrong, the second paragraph is easy to change.

---

**The Toast**

Good evening, everyone. For those who don't know me, I'm [YOUR NAME], Dan's brother, which means I've known him longest and have the most material. Don't worry, [PARTNER], I've picked only the good stuff.

Dan and [PARTNER] met in college. Even then, Dan was already the guy everyone called. Broken bike? Call Dan. Dead laptop? Dan. Bad breakup, worse resume, a car that wouldn't start in January? Dan, Dan, Dan. He never made a big deal of it. He'd just show up with a toolbox, or a casserole, or the right questions. Dan fixes things. It's who he is.

So when he decided to propose, I wasn't worried about whether he'd do it well. I was worried about the location. He chose a frozen lake in Minnesota. In winter. Where the entire plan depended on the one thing Dan can't fix: ice.

Now, I'm told it was about ten degrees out. I'm told there was a lot of shivering and some very emotional, very cold tears. And I'm told [PARTNER] said yes before Dan had even finished the question. That tells me [PARTNER] had already figured out what the rest of us learned long ago. When Dan shows up, things get better.

[PARTNER], here's what I've noticed. Dan has spent his whole life fixing things for other people. You're the first person who makes him want to stop fixing and just enjoy something. I've never seen him happier, or, honestly, more relaxed. Thank you for that.

Dan, you've always had our backs. Today, we've got yours.

So please raise a glass. To Dan and [PARTNER]: may your love be solid, your winters be short, and if anything ever does break, may you still be the two people each of you calls first.

Cheers!

---

**To make it yours**

- **Add one real story.** A toast lands best with one specific, true detail. For example, what Dan actually fixed for you, or a moment you saw him with [PARTNER]. Swap it in for the "Broken bike? Call Dan" list if you have a better one.
- **Check the ice joke.** If the proposal story has a known detail, like a fishing shack, ice skates, or a ring dropped in the snow, work it in. Guests love hearing the real version.
- **Pauses.** Stop for a beat after "ice." and after "Dan fixes things." The jokes need that room to land.
- **Practice out loud.** Time yourself twice. If you run long, cut the "Thank you for that" paragraph down to one sentence.
- **Hold the glass until the last line.** Raise it at "So please raise a glass."

If you send me [PARTNER]'s name, one real story about Dan, and how formal the crowd is, I can tailor it further.
